svg.title: A secure zone is the wrong diagram; the trust boundary inventory is the right artifact
svg.desc: Left: the diagram that gets drawn, a dashed box labelled secure zone around core, server, switch and firewall, assuming everything inside is safe and everything outside is hostile. It enforces nothing and hides the flows that actually matter. Right: the artifact that gets built, six boundary relationships with the direction of the trust change and the control each one needs. Employee endpoint to internal server, low to high, needs authentication plus authorization plus inspection. Branch to headquarters, low to high, needs an encrypted tunnel plus policy. Operations staff to network devices, medium to highest, needs a bastion, two factors and audit. DMZ to internal, lowest to high, must be one-way and default deny. Partner to one service, external to a subset, needs one-way extranet access and least privilege. Office to production, needs isolation with no lateral movement allowed. A footer states the inventory is page one of the design, the device list is page four.
svg.text: A zone is a surface. A trust boundary is an edge. Only the edge enforces anything.
Left: the diagram that gets drawn. Right: the artifact that gets built.
and nothing in between is described
This box enforces nothing. It cannot say
who may talk to whom, and it hides the
flows that matter: the vendor link, the
operations path, the DMZ return traffic.
An incident travels along a relationship,
WHAT GETS BUILT - SIX EDGES, SIX CONTROLS
encrypted tunnel + policy, not trust by default
one-way, default deny, no return path initiated
one-way extranet access, least privilege, logged
isolation, no lateral path in either direction
Every row here becomes an ACL, a zone pair, a VRF or a segmentation tag later - and every row has an owner, because a boundary
without an owner is a boundary nobody maintains.
Page order in the design document: assets, then boundaries and flows, then controls, then devices. The device list is page four.
